rationale: B wins because it edits: three real beats, each with the proof test that would make or break the pitch. Its line "Without the code-quality proof this angle gets torn apart on contact" is the adult in the room; A's "Figma just picked a fight with every AI tool that turns a prompt into an app" is punchy but drags in a competitive market the supplied facts did not establish. A has useful material, but it pads into shakier labor and competitive claims where B stays disciplined.
gaps_in_A: "Figma just picked a fight with every AI tool that turns a prompt into an app" overstates the competitive field; the update gives product capabilities, not a mapped prompt-to-app market.
"dominated by smaller AI-native code-generation startups" is imported context, not a supplied fact. If you need that market claim, prove it or cut it.
"The Adobe deal died. Figma's answer was to launch its biggest bet yet" piles causality and magnitude onto one thin fact: the launch followed the deal collapse.
"the first time the question has real stakes rather than being hypothetical" in the junior-developer angle is too grand. The update has no labor data, hiring signal, or adoption proof.
gaps_in_B: "first big swing since the Adobe deal died" is still unsupported. The update says the launch follows the collapse, not that it is first, biggest, or explicitly strategic.
"what does Figma do now that the exit is gone" is a loaded corporate-frame leap. It may be true newsroom shorthand, but the facts only say no IPO timing was disclosed.
The next step, "journalist-fit-check," is premature if no target names exist yet. Build the beat list first, then fit-check names against the chosen angle.
The AI assistant fact is underused. B folds "generates layouts from a text prompt" into the handoff story but never tests whether that assistant is itself a distinct design-workflow angle.
